Sara Klaniczay  

Oedipal fantasies; boundaries; puberty; truancy and vagrancy; enactment and symbolisation.

This paper is about the therapy of a runaway boy in early adolescence. A series of such incidents, which spanned a year of his life, was closely connected with his sexual maturation and oedipal situation. It was of great importance to the author that four of those incidents happened during the therapy, thus giving the opportunity to observe in statu nascendi, so to speak.

A further interesting feature of this case was that the patient committed a crime — codified as ‘Unauthorized Crossing of the Frontier’ — and this represented his incestuous desires. Realizing the underlying phantasy helped the author to form her interpretation, which became a turning point in the therapy. The activity driving the boy into running away diminished, and the compulsive whirlpool-like symptoms ceased.

Searching for psychological ‘models’ was considered by Imre Hermann as very important in our therapeutic work and also in creativity-research.

The analysis of ‘model’ connections teaches us that the special shape of individual problems is formed both by the conflicts of instincts and by socio-psychological factors embedded in wide-ranging social movements.

The two questions on the back cover of the book provide a succinct reflection of the aim of this book: What are the main features of contemporary psychoanalysis? What do the different schools of psychoanalysis have in common?

197

In the introduction the authors state that psychoanalysis is in crisis: struggling to differentiate itself from psychoanalytic psychotherapy and ‘its other offspring’, seeking new forms of leadership, being threatened by economic recession, diversifying and coming under increasing scrutiny from all directions. Hence the book's focus on contemporary psychoanalytic theory and an attempt to find unity and common ground within the movement. In order to place the contemporary issues in context, a brief history of psychoanalysis is offered, with a ‘family tree of psychoanalysis’: who analysed whom. I found this intriguing and I wish I had seen it much earlier on in my training.

The authors aim to present the similarities and differences between the various schools of psychoanalytic thought, believing that clinical theory can be unified in a meaningful way despite theoretical divergence. They argue that clinicians need to have a particular analytic perspective from which to work but that they should be able to draw on a range of different ideas and techniques. This appealed to me, perhaps because of the nature of my training (at the British Association of Psychotherapists), but I wondered whether the book would be able to rise to such a challenge.

The work is in the tradition of the ‘critical dictionary’ (Rycroft, 1972; Hinshelwood, 1989) in that it aims to clarify and question in order to extract what is valuable from each psychoanalytic viewpoint. As a trainee about to embark on the final stages of training, I was curious to find out if it would be rich enough to satisfy my needs at this point, and yet not be so complex that I could derive benefit from it only years after qualifying.

The book is organized into two sections. The first deals with contemporary psychoanalytic theory, covering theories of development, transference and countertransference, defence mechanisms and models of the mind. The second section deals with practice: this includes psychoanalytic technique, the application of psychoanalytic ideas to the treatment of psychiatric illness, and psychoanalytic research.

John Woods  

I would like to express my appreciation of the article ‘AIDS and the unconscious: psychodynamic group work with incarcerated youths’ which appeared in Vol. 23 No. 3, December 1997. It is an excellent account of exciting and innovative work in a much needed area. Though from the other side of the globe it is in tune with increased concern and activity in this locality with the same patient population, viz for example the Bulletin of the ACP of the same month which contains several very useful contributions from child psychotherapists working in relation to legal systems, and also the planned ACP Scientific Meeting on January entitled ‘Loss and Delinquency: Two Adolescents’ Experiences of Prison as an External Container for Psychic Pain’, speaker Debbie Hindle.

As psychoanalytic psychotherapists move away from the protected environment of the private or clinic based consulting room the threats to our professional identity and integrity grow stronger. We are very much in need of demonstrable evidence of the value of our work. Recently I was asked to review a set of three new books by psychologists on work with juvenile sex offenders, none of which gave any regard to ‘psychodynamic theory’. But experience shows that cognitive-behavioural treatment strategies, while providing structure, containment and perhaps above all, rationality for the therapists, may very likely fail to engage with the unconsciously determined (and they are determined!) forces that work toward the destructiveness of these young people. However, the most effective ‘CBT’ therapists that I know seem to have an intuitive grasp of defensive processes such as resistance, splitting and projection and an awareness of the emotional needs for these. These therapists though not officially ‘psychoanalytic’ will also tolerate and use re-enactments of trauma within a transference relationship. They may not interpret such processes as such but do allow, I believe, therapeutic internal change to take place at an emotional and experiential level.

Editorial

Judith Edwards , Monica Lanyado and Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

The issues arising from the development of Freud's original formulation of the Oedipus complex continue to expand, and we open this August 1998 edition of the journal with a paper by Anne Alvarez, ‘Failures to link: attacks or defects? Some questions concerning the thinkability of Oedipal and pre-Oedipal thoughts’. In this paper the author offers an extension of the territory of our theoretical landscape by exploring Bion's theory of thinking. She points out some contradictions, and suggests ways in which what she calls ‘the modulating present object’ helps the infant move towards sequentiality, ordinality and twoness, as a precursor to the concept of absence and the notion of three. In the December Klein memorial edition we shall be publishing two further papers which take the Oedipus complex as their starting point.

The second paper in this edition was presented in an earlier form to the 1997 Annual Conference of the Association of Child Psychotherapists. In ‘Dialogues with parents’, Margaret Rustin offers an overview of current clinical approaches to psychoanalytically informed work with parents. As she points out, child psychotherapists, by virtue of their sensitivity to infantile features in the personality, possess a particular and proper basis for psychoanalytic psychotherapeutic work with parents, and this represents a shift in professional identity.

There has been much controversy surrounding the diagnosis and treatment of children thought to be suffering from ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) and it is now two years since there began, in this journal, a correspondence on the issues involved. In this edition we publish two papers which extend and inform this important debate. In ‘Wrestling with the whirlwind’, Eileen Orford describes some of the difficulties involved in making a correct diagnosis of ADD/ADHD and how it tends to be an over-diagnosed condition. Careful attention needs to be paid to each child's situation so that an understanding of the causes of their behaviour can be reached.

Cathy Urwin  

Until relatively recently, it has been easy to assume that the experimental methods favoured by psychology have precluded developmental studies of such subjective phenomena as emotion. Over the last ten to fifteen years or so, developmental psychologists have increasingly given more attention to emotional processes and their relation to other aspects of development, turning experimental expertise to great advantage. Over the same time period, psychotherapists have shown greater interest in the work of developmental psychologists, to gain greater insight into so-called ‘normal’ development. This, for example, is to enrich our understanding of the tasks to be faced by very disturbed children, and is part of a general imperative to build better models of the mind and its objects. These are fed by emotional relationships and our engagements with them.

This book represents a synthesis of work in developmental psychology carried out by the author and his colleagues, which had its inception in follow-up studies on attachment begun in the 1970s. Broadly speaking, it puts forward the thesis that emotional life in early childhood is organized in two inter-related senses.

Firstly, emotions, such as pleasure, fear, anger, shame, affection and guilt, form part of integrating developing systems which emerge according to hierarchical principles. Second, emotional experience itself depends on the development of the regulation of tension, or arousal, produced by external or internal stimulation. This principle is linked to the first via the postulate that, while some degree of tension is necessary in order to function efficiently, whether or not an emotion can or does occur depends on the infant's capacity to generate tension and to tolerate it.

Editorial

Judith Edwards and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

Following the special editions on Anna Freud (Vol. 21, No. 3), Michael Fordham (Vol. 22, No. 1) and Donald Winnicott (Vol. 22, No. 3), we are very pleased to be publishing an edition of the journal commemorating the life and work of Melanie Klein. As will be evident from the various contributions in this volume, Melanie Klein's thinking has been seminal and continues to have a significant influence on contemporary practitioners.

Melanie Klein (1882-1960) started work as a psychoanalyst at the end of the First World War in 1919, and when she died in 1960 she was still working clinically and developing theoretically. In her innovative work she expanded initially on the thinking of her mentor Sigmund Freud, and then began to diverge from him, offering profound new thoughts about mental processes and the primitive infantile phantasies which lie at the core of psychic life. A pioneer of object relations theory, she paved the way towards working with more disturbed patients, and was the first analyst to recognize that there was symbolic significance in children's play. She was a person and a thinker who aroused strong emotions; her ideas resulted in controversies which are still active today. We hope that this edition of the journal will give a sense of perspective in consideration of her life and work, and go some way towards illustrating both the complexities of her thinking and its continued relevance in our work with children, as child psychotherapists around the world understanding the concepts of Melanie Klein in clinical ways. This edition is not of course an exhaustive account of previous or contemporary thinking: we remain conscious of other rich contributions to the evolution of the history of ideas, including, for instance, those of Dr Donald Meltzer. Perhaps this edition will prompt current practitioners and thinkers to offer papers which may fill the inevitable gaps in this memorial issue.

We open with a paper by Hanna Segal, who was analysed by Melanie Klein and then became a co-worker. Together with Rosenfeld, Dr Segal was one of the first to analyse psychotic patients using Kleinian concepts.

Melanie Klein; psychoanalytic teaching; teaching theory; projective identification.

I shall attempt to bring together here thoughts of experienced clinicians and teachers who have taught Melanie Klein's theories to child psychotherapists. However, most of the contributors have also taught Klein to clinical trainees in adult psychoanalytic work and to different groups abroad and, in some cases, to already trained psychotherapists or psychoanalysts. Klein's theories are introduced at different stages in the different child psychotherapy programmes in London. For instance, the students at the Tavistock are introduced to Klein's theories before they are necessarily in their own psychoanalysis, while other trainings introduce her theories in the introductory years of the clinical training.

William Halton is one of the longest-running teachers of Klein in the Tavistock Child Psychotherapy Training and brings his ‘framework’ culled from many years of experience. Maria Rhode has taught the Narrative to students at the Tavistock for many years. Elizabeth Spillius, psychoanalyst, writer and teacher, brings her experiences teaching Klein to non-Kleinians. Karen Proner teaches at the Tavistock, in Italy and the United States.

My main difficulty with Roger Kennedy's book is an uncertainty about the intended readership. The early chapters seem to be aimed at a wide range of professionals. They are written largely in non-technical language and communicate complex psychoanalytic themes clearly and simply as they are relevant to work with the very disturbed families who are

468

referred to the Family Unit at the Cassel Hospital. The facilities provided there for in-patient observation, assessment and treatment for whole families are exceptional, and Roger Kennedy does an excellent job of describing, perhaps to potential referrers, how the unit works and for which types of family it may work most successfully. He gives excellent case examples to illustrate his themes, and refers to relevant research succinctly. These early chapters have all appeared in other journals, but hold together well, in spite of some repetitions which could have been removed by tighter editing. The core chapter of the book, ‘A complete case history’, is a moving account of the careful and thoughtful way in which the multi-disciplinary staff of the unit work together through referral and in-patient treatment to rehabilitation at home of a mother and child. There is particular emphasis in this chapter on the role of the nurse therapists. Thereafter come some newly written chapters which have a more explicit psychoanalytic base. Here the language changes. In the chapter on ‘The abused child, the abused adult and recovered memories of abuse’ Roger Kennedy describes in some detail his work in his psychoanalytic practice with an adult patient who had been sexually abused as a child. This chapter was previously published in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and it could provide a useful balance for therapists with adults by detailing the Cassel experience with abused adults and children. However, the earlier chapters are less likely to sustain the interest of psychotherapists, and the unevenness of the collage does finally disappoint this reviewer.

There is bound to be a tension when writing about an area of work which is essentially at an interface — between internal phantasies and external realities; between the individual and the family; between the family and the therapeutic work of the institution; between the institution and the complex professional and legal network surrounding the family: that is, between being over-psychoanalytic and therefore inaccessible to a wide range of other professionals, and not being psychoanalytic enough for the more psychoanalytically based clinician. Ultimately in this book I feel Kennedy addresses the former, for whom he provides thoughtful reflections based on his extensive experience as Consultant Psychotherapist at the Cassel.

When Bertha Pappenheim took to her bed on 11 December 1880, she made a big impact on the history of ideas. The story of Bertha's treatment (‘Fraulein Anna O.’) and its abrupt termination in June 1882 inaugurated the beginnings of a revolutionary shift in the mind of her

462

physician's young assistant, Sigmund Freud. What led the senior Doctor, Breuer, to flee (Bertha's comment, while writhing with abdominal cramps on that fateful summer's evening, ‘Now Dr. B's child is coming!’) led the other to conceive psychoanalysis. What Breuer recoiled from, the traditional version goes, Freud examined, and discovered transference.

From the vantage point of more than a century later, it is possible to redescribe this, as both John Forrester (1990) and Peter Gay (1988: 63-9) have done, not in the one-way-street language of transference (the patient transfers, the analyst is evenly suspended) but in the living intersubjective language of transference-countertransference dialectics. Breuer, these authors argue, not only fled from the potentially scandalous appearance of Bertha's erotic fantasies about him, but from the still more scandalogenic jolt of recognition that his interest in her was not merely medical. The erotic dimension, stirred into conscious apprehension by Bertha's remarks (although it had been detected previously by his wife), terrified him and he abandoned the treatment.

As Robert Young (1994) has remarked, if transference is projection, countertransference is projective identification — something elicited by the patient in the therapist: evocative, as opposed to didactic, knowledge. The richly evocative collection of papers edited by Tsiantis, Sandler, Anastasopoulos and Martindale in this volume shows how psychoanalytic thinkers and practitioners from different schools are working, from different perspectives, within a new paradigm. This is dialectical science, the science of intersubjectivity. As Jessica Benjamin (1995) has written, agreement on the importance of the two-person field, where learning from and articulating the countertransference in the here-and-now relationship is the central focus, may turn out to be a rather more essential point than disagreements about the make-up of the one-person field.

The title and cover photos of this book (clumpy lace-up boots in black and white) convey something of an orthodox, even plodding, approach to this well-worked subject. You do not have to read too far however to have such a preconception overturned. This is far from orthodox, and plodding it is not. The author, a psychoanalytic child and adolescent psychotherapist, quickly dismisses a view of adolescence based on a ‘teleology of developmental tasks … kick-started by puberty’. Such theories for ‘ordering the unorderable’ are nonsense, he suggests, and ‘our developmental timetables’ are better used like those we peruse at the bus-stop — ‘not to be taken seriously but serving as a distraction while we wait’.

While setting the iconoclastic tone of the book, the author does stop short of completely debunking mainstream psychoanalytic theory, much of which is brilliant and inspirational, he says, ‘but it needs to be liberated from its confinement to the years between short trousers and long skirts’. This sentence is one possible key to the book, which, if I have understood it at all, seeks to establish adolescence as a state of mind resident in the human psyche at any age and not projectively confined by the adult majority to the young people to whom we normally attach such a label.

This book defies easy classification or definition. Its theme may be said to be a combination of two linked ideas.

You have asked me to comment on the three papers from Eastern Europe on child psychotherapy in Russia and Hungary, which appeared in the previous issue, as I have been working there, mainly in Russia and the Ukraine, on a regular basis over the past eleven years. My experience reflects exactly the themes of the papers, particularly what Kagan calls “the post totalitarian stress syndrome” — the sudden disintegration of a well established way of life, which has generated a high level of anxiety and psychological conflict. It seems to me to be a good phrase to help to explain how different people react so differently to the consequences of the collapse of the Soviet Union, each according to their own degree of resilience and social support as with other traumatised people in different situations. For what else but traumatic is the pain of everyday life in the C.I.S. where there is high inflation, scarce resources, little personal money, (some Civil Servants haven't been paid for years let alone months); high unemployment, a crumbling infrastructure, (including fragmentation of the once unified health system into fifteen new ones, each with reduced resources including equipment and in particular medicines); an old ideology which can no longer cope with current needs and change hampered by rigid, hierarchic and beaurocratic organisational structures. There is deterioration in the diets of most of the population, leading to seventy percent of new born babies having a pathological condition and twenty one out of a thousand teenagers who “enter adult life with an illness” Ryan (1993). Nina Vasilyeva's case history traces in detail the tragic effects of these statistics on one family and the courage and determination needed in trying to work in such a situation. She also shows that using a psychodynamic model of treatment, (regularity, individual work, boundary setting, transference etc) can be helpful, even in such cases.

I should like to comment on the interesting and innovative paper by Gunnar Carlsberg, ‘Laughter opens the door: turning points in child psychotherapy’ in the previous issue of this journal.

The author noticed that in the course of individual psychodynamic therapy with children, therapists often identified particular sessions where something qualitatively new occurred. He set out to research these ‘significant points’ with a view to increasing knowledge about processes of change. Critical of the usual outcome studies, he makes a case for a research method which ‘taps the rich clinical experience of skilled therapists — and which is in harmony with the psychotherapy process itself’.

The research was based on interviews with five therapists who were asked to make contact if they experienced one of these turning points in the course of their work. The therapists were then asked to produce process notes for the turning point session and for the two preceding sessions, to answer a questionnaire and also were interviewed one and two years later. A number of narratives were thus collected, which were analysed to discover common themes and underlying patterns.

This original paper raised many questions in my mind. I found myself wondering how many of my own cases, past and present, showed these turning points. Some did but in others, retrospectively I could not think of any. What about those steady, plodding cases where nothing new seems to happen yet some gradual change occurs? An advantage of this kind of research is that it encourages us to think about processes of change and to try to formulate what we are doing. A disadvantage seems to be the unpredictability of these turning points where surprise is a crucial element.

There is certainly a need for innovative methods of research.

In this paper, work with two adolescents from different families, each of whom lost their same-sex parent in tragic circumstances, is described. Inpatient psychotherapy; psychosocial nursing; Cassel Hospital; Munchhausen syndrome by proxy; severe psychopathology.

This paper looks at the experience of inpatient hospital treatment at the Cassel Hospital and how formal psychoanalytic psychotherapy, with its emphasis on the transference and the inner world, fits into that context and orientates itself to some of the realities of the setting. It outlines how psychotherapy and nursing can work to inform and enrich each other, and what is psychoanalytic about the overall work. A bridge of understanding is built using the patients' perceptions of, adjustment to and conflict about the inpatient setting, and the affective impact of the processes on patients and staff alike. Two clinical examples of severe child abuse family cases are given, the first of Munchhausen syndrome by proxy, the second in which a baby sibling had been killed. They show how in-depth psychoanalytic work with mother and child and individual psychotherapy of the child can be combined with psychotherapy of the parents and intensive work in the therapeutic community. Such a combination can contribute, even in cases of severe pathology, to the development of the relationship between mother and child and promote successful rehabilitation in the outside community.

In the myth of Oedipus there are numerous narrations of the Oedipus complex, where the most primitive levels are interwoven with the most evolved ones. The author describes the impact of political thought on the theory and practice of child psychotherapy in Russia since the 1920s. The Child's Experience of Munchhausen Syndrome by Proxy

Deirdre Dowling

Deirdre Dowling

61 The Ridings
Surbiton KT5 8HG

Deirdre Dowling  

Munchhausen syndrome by proxy; child psychotherapy; trauma.

This paper examines the emotional impact of Munchhausen syndrome by proxy on a child aged 6 who had been poisoned by her mother. It describes her treatment in child psychotherapy over twenty months at the Cassel Hospital where the family worked towards her successful rehabilitation home. The work with her showed her experience of dangerous relationships in her family that left her distrustful of any new relationship, and doubtful of her capacity to be close without being destructive. Like her parents, she was terrified of facing the murderous feelings in the family, retreating into denial when life was too painful. The paper describes three phases of treatment: fear of separation and preoccupation with the trauma of poisoning, ambivalence about facing the destructiveness in the family and the move into more appropriate latency behaviour as she prepared to go home with her parents. It concludes with an overview of the impact of Munchhausen syndrome by proxy on the developing child, as shown in this treatment: the delay in emotional and cognitive development, the interference with the capacity to relate, the retreat into illness under stress, and the fear of permanent damage caused by the emotional and physical abuse.

This book is based on papers presented at the Tavistock Conference on Infant Observation held in 1993. The function of the conference, and of this book which originated from it, was to allow the exploration and review of the developments that had taken place in infant observation — both theoretical developments that had arisen from it and changes in clinical practice that it had informed.

The book is divided into three parts: Part I describes the practice of infant observation; Part II deals with new conceptual developments which have arisen out of infant observation; Part III describes the application of infant observation for the purposes of research. In her excellent introduction, Susan Reid provides a clear description of the method of infant observation, the experience of becoming an observer, the role of the infant observation seminar and the rationale and applications of the method to many clinical trainings.

In Part I, interesting examples are given of infant observation. Isca Wittenberg makes many astute observations on the process of infant observation and, in particular, gives us some insight into the experience of being a seminar leader of an infant observation group. Jeanne Magagna's chapter on the nanny-parent interaction provides insights into the various shared internal images which develop in the mother-nanny-baby relationship. She then goes on to provide fascinating examples of each of the categories of shared internal images which she has described. Lynda Ellis's chapter on the meaning of difference explores infant observation as a tool for studying ‘differentness’ and highlights what a sensitive tool it is for doing this.

In Part II, the way in which theoretical developments can spring from infant observation are described.

Tamar Fransman  

In this book Joan and Neville Symington have two aims: to reach the ‘psychoanalytically educated’ reader who wants to understand the main tenets of Bion's thinking and to encourage and inform the clinician who wishes to apply Bion's thinking to his or her work. In doing so (the latter in particular) they are filling a gap in the literature on Bion. In the preface they assert that Bion's thinking differs radically from that of previous psychoanalytical thinkers and that he is ‘the deepest thinker within psychoanalysis’ (p. xii). The authors explain how Bion shifted the emphasis of psychoanalysis from a study of the emotional and the pathological aspects of mental life to mental life involved with thinking and thought processes. This change of emphasis applies to the clinician as well as his patient so that the mind of the clinician is as much a subject of study as that of his patient and the relationship between the patient and clinician. Furthermore, the Symingtons hope to inspire clinicians in another crucial area of Bion's thinking, namely to tolerate not knowing or understanding. They feel the success of their book is dependent on the extent to which they can persuade their readers to leave the sides of the known and jump into the ‘terror’ (p. 184) of the unknown.

Unlike many other books which explore Bion's work biographically or through the development of his theories (for example, Bleandonu, 1994; Grinberg et al., 1975; Meltzer, 1978), the Symingtons structure their book around Bion's grid.

Editorial

Monica Lanyado and Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

This edition of the journal contains papers on a variety of clinical subjects as well as a special section on child psychotherapy in Russia and Hungary. Whatever part of the world child psychotherapists practise in, they are working within a specific social and political context. When this context is relatively benign, there is an assumption that free thought is a clinical right. It is therefore of great interest to hear about what has happened to clinical practice and theoretical thinking in countries where freedom of thought was politically severely limited for many years. This special section addresses some of these questions.

Catalina Bronstein and Sara Flanders' paper ‘The development of a therapeutic space in a first contact with adolescents’, presented at the Second European Conference on Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in Stockholm in September 1996, is a careful and thought-provoking description and clinical demonstration of their work with this notoriously difficult client group. Based on work developed at a walk-in centre, where adolescents in a state of crisis refer themselves, the theoretical foundations of the work are explored, and more detailed work with two adolescents is described as they become able to think about their difficulties in the contained space of a therapeutic consultation.

The theme of working with difficult adolescents is continued in Deborah Hindle's paper ‘Loss and delinquency: two adolescents’ experience of prison as an external container for psychic pain'. The author describes her work with two adolescent patients who were imprisoned during the course of their treatment. Both had suffered the tragic loss of their same-sex parent and the author discusses how this loss may have affected their ability to establish an ‘inner authority’. The paper describes these unusual treatments before, during and after imprisonment and emphasizes the importance of the professional network in which therapy took place. This fascinating account raises interesting questions about the role of the therapist in cases such as these, and the setting in which therapy can take place.

Angela Joyce  

This is an ambitious book, albeit modestly presented as a preliminary and exploratory attempt to bridge the gap between psychoanalytic theorizing and empirical methods. The literature on baby observation from a psychoanalytic perspective is slim, but growing, and the author of this

187

volume goes beyond the more usual presentation of a single case study. Stephen Briggs modifies the infant observation method, pioneered by Esther Bick as part of the training in child psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic, into a research instrument, by developing categories for comparison, and by focusing on a group of infants deemed to be vulnerable or ‘at risk’. He seeks to ‘operationalize’ Bion's theory of the ‘container-contained’, and Bick's ‘skin formation’, and through this to provide a ‘grid’, comparing five observed babies, over a two-year period. He is interested to see if the kind of containment offered by the mother (and other family members who care for an infant), and what he describes as the ‘grip relations’ established by the baby, have observable consequences in the child's life, and especially to consider the relationship between emotion and cognition. Among his various aims he seeks to develop research instruments to predict resilience and risk, and to generate new psychoanalytic theory through the application of these instruments.

This is a study rich in material for comment, and I cannot do justice to it in a short review. However, I will try to spell out what I see as valuable, as well as the many problems I had in reading this book. I will group the difficulties I had into three: 1) the problem of theoretical preconceptions; 2) the claim to be extending psychoanalytic theory together with the narrowness of the theory used; 3) other issues connected with the methodology.

The issue of the influence of theoretical preconceptions on what is perceived and understood through observation is central: the potential for one's observations to be made and conceptualized in ways which fit in with pre-existing theory is great. You see what your theory sees, and not what it does not see; ontology is confused with epistemology. Briggs tries to deal with this, referring to notions of ‘transcendental realism’ (Bhaskar, 1978) and ‘grounded theory’ (Glaser and Strauss, 1971). Using Bick's method of observation in which there is no prestructured protocol, the richness of the data recorded, he says, provides for the generation of substantive theory, new approaches and perspectives. And there is some limited evidence for this in Briggs' accounts of the five case studies. However, the point about Glaser and Strauss' ideas is that research too often contains a priori assumptions which mask important features of reality. ‘Research must instead be used to generate “grounded” theories which, rather than forcing data into a preconceived “objective” reality, would seek to mobilise as an explanatory tool, the categories which the participants themselves use to order their experience’ (Silverman, 1970). In my view, Briggs too often forces his data into his own preconceived theoretical reality.

Trudy Klauber

Trudy Klauber

Child and Family Department, Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Trudy Klauber  

Parents of autistic, psychotic and atypical children; trauma; post-traumatic stress; strain trauma, parenting capacities; parent-work; parent psychotherapy.

Living with disturbed children is seen as traumatizing to vulnerable parents, who identify their disturbed child with trauma so that their parental functioning is disrupted and parenting capacities lost or impaired. This paper links Tischler's thoughts on work with the parents of psychotic and autistic children with more recent work by Garland on the impact of trauma on psychic function in adults, suggesting that the personal disaster of having and living with such children is as traumatizing as a major public one. Those who undertake work with parents need to be sensitive to their impact on parents who may feel further traumatized rather than supported. It is suggested that an understanding of post-traumatic stress phenomena may increase the sensitivity of the child psychotherapist to these hypervigilant parents who so quickly feel persecuted. Commitment to work with parents often needs to be long-term. Well-established trust allows the worker to move between levels in the work, from that of giving support and advice around specific difficulties to more truly analytic work with individual parents or couples in which they may come to understand how some of their own history may be projected into the vulnerable child.

Maria Lupinacci  

Parental couple; Oedipal phantasies; triangular space; countertransference.

The author refers to the parental couple as it appears in relation to the Oedipus complex at the various levels of development and psychical maturation. A ‘pathological’ Oedipus situation is differentiated from a ‘normal’ one. Accordingly the author distinguishes the primitive Oedipal fantasies about the parental couple represented in the myth by the parents of Thebes and the parents of Corinth (and the influence that these can have on the psychoanalytic work), from a couple who have reached truly creative functioning. Furthermore, it is pointed out how elements are activated in the therapist's mind: emotional qualities of a feminine maternal and masculine paternal kind that either collaborate in containing and promoting the psychoanalytic process and psychic development of the patient or else fail in this task.

Judith Jackson  

Transference; total situation; countertransference.

This paper describes and examines further Klein's (1952) view that it is essential to recognize that total situations are transferred from the past into the present and need to be considered alongside emotions, defences and object relations in unravelling and understanding the nature of the unfolding transference. Two clinical vignettes, taken from work with children, highlight specific difficulties in dealing with intensely uncomfortable and quite complex countertransference experiences which were eventually understood only when the total situation of the patient's internal experience of his infancy and early childhood and the projection of defences, affects and object relations could be linked.

Trevor Lubbe

Trevor Lubbe

36 Carstens Street

South Africa

Trevor Lubbe  

Projective identification, identification by projection, projection, work with children,

Since its introduction by Melanie Klein in 1946 the concept of projective identification has inspired, baffled, rankled, but always mesmerized its adherents and opponents alike. I offer in this paper a brief outline of the concept's development over the past fifty years by way of some thoughts on a personal journey of discovery surrounding its meaning and clinical usefulness to my work as a child therapist. I would like to suggest that definitions in current use seem to be derived more from adult work than from work with children, which has sometimes skewed the debate surrounding the concept in a particular direction. In both its conceptual guises, namely, as an unconscious ‘phantasy’ and as an interpersonal feature of the transference, projective identification is a logical extension of certain aspects of Klein's work with small children. In child work too the developmental status of the concept comes more into focus.

This paper describes work done in the voluntary sector under the auspices of the Catholic Children's Society (Westminster). Based on the Tavistock's Under-5s model, whole families are offered a series of up to five meetings to explore their difficulties. This paper is based on work developed at a walk-in centre for adolescents. Our initial approach is one which involves, on the one hand, assessing the adolescent's difficulties and, on the other, encouraging the development of a therapeutic experience. Interviewing, in form and intent, aims to address the adolescent's anxieties about needing help and to counter the omnipotent adolescent defences with the establishment of a therapeutic space and the development of commitment to its use. It provides an experience of containment through understanding and opens the possibility of the creation of a space for thinking. Unless there is some development in this capacity, and some understanding of the anxieties that made the adolescent ask for help, there is little prospect of the adolescent being able to sustain ongoing psychotherapy or psychoanalysis.

The first part of this paper, by the first author, focuses on the theoretical foundations of this work and also explores the crucial role that the institution has in this initial contact with adolescents. The second part, by the second author, provides a more detailed look at the interviewing of two adolescents who, with their very different character structures and histories, show anxiety about therapy or analysis that is specific to adolescent experience, particularly fears of being passively overwhelmed due to the threatened loss of an omnipotent defence which had been established to cope with adolescent change.

Cathy Urwin

Cathy Urwin

Ground Floor Flat

Cathy Urwin  

Premature birth; parental divorce; psychoanalytic psychotherapy; trauma; containment.

This paper illustrates a relationship between the containment of anxiety and the capacity to work through and recover from traumatic events as it emerged in the once weekly psychotherapy of an 8-year-old boy, born three months prematurely. At referral his presentation strongly suggested the impact of his parents' separation and subsequent divorce three years previously, and the implications of being unable to express, comprehend and work through his feelings. He was depressed, disillusioned and caught up in deception and self-destructive behaviour. However, as the psychotherapy progressed, the significance of his premature birth came into the foreground. This had impeded his establishing a containing function in infancy. A major contribution of the psychotherapy was to create the possibility for primitive anxiety to be thought about and to some extent made bearable. This contributed to a greater capacity for thinking reflectively, for dialogue with others, and for modifying harsh internal figures. The implications of the parents' divorce could then be worked through more adequately. Due to external pressures on the parents, the therapy was terminated after four terms with a planned ending. Though this was itself in many respects premature, a review six months later indicated sustained changes in the child's ability to relate to his parents and in his capacity to regulate his anxiety and think reflectively.

Anmarie Widener  

ADD, ADHD, children, parents, psychotherapy, Ritalin,

It is estimated that as many as 5 million children in America are being medicated with psycho-stimulants for Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD) and/or Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Parents frequently seek psychotherapy for their child up to one and a half years after medication has been tried due to a high degree of symptom recidivism. The parents should be engaged in the therapeutic work, if at all possible. An intricate web begins to unfold as the current parent-child relationship resonates with the parents' relationship with their own parents, siblings and childhood experiences. Working with the parents is essential if one is going to know anything about the cross-generational dynamics involved and if real and helpful change is going to occur. Conscious and unconscious parent-child dynamics of hyperactive behaviour in children are discussed. A clinical case illustration is described. Alternatives to medicating children are also described.

This paper offers an overview of current clinical approaches to psychoanalytically informed work with parents by child psychotherapists. The analysis is based on practice at the Tavistock Clinic and on broader knowledge of trends in work with children and families within the National Health Service. A brief history sets the scene. Four varieties of approach are described, with clinical examples. The particular sensitivity of child psychotherapists to infantile features in the personality is highlighted, and it is argued that this, together with their broad clinical experience, provides a proper basis for psychoanalytic psychotherapy with parents. Such work significantly extends and enriches the clinical contribution of child psychotherapists and has involved a shift in professional identity. It also raises ethical issues which are discussed.

In this contribution I examine Klein's 1930 paper ‘The importance of symbol-formation in the development of the ego’, and try to show that it is one of her most important and seminal papers. In the paper she boldly states that the capacity for symbol formation is crucial in the development of the ego. She links it with the development of object relationships, and emphasizes the role of aggression and anxiety as well as the libido. It foreshadows her concept of projective identification. The paper opened a new area of investigation: it was seminal in provoking new developments and in furthering understanding of psychotic disturbances in the development of thinking and sublimation.

The paper addresses the psychoanalytic question of how the child comes to know reality, especially a reality which demands two-tracked thinking. Some contradictions in Bion's theories of thinking are observed. Where there is a real difficulty or deficit in making links, rather than an attack on a previously established link, the therapist may need to attend to certain temporal and dynamic features of the link which can enable sequentiality, ordinality and twoness to be bearable and pleasurable. Bobbie Akinboro-Cooper  

Michael Vannoy Adams' personal experiences have nurtured a creative awareness of multiculturalism. Though this thought-provoking book is based on multicultural life in America, the issues are also relevant to multicultural life in Britain. Adams works in private practice as a psychotherapist, defining himself as a pluralist, respecting all the schools of psychoanalytic thought, but declaring an interest in Jungian analysis. The author is also a senior lecturer in psychoanalytic studies at the New School for Social Research, in New York.

Generally, Adams' book is about, ‘race, color, and the unconscious and the prospects for a multicultural psychoanalysis’. His specific interest is in the collective dimensions of, what he defines as, projective typifications (i.e. stereotypical projections ‘as they appear both consciously and unconsciously in the personal experience of the individual’).

Adams guides us confidently through psychoanalytic explorations of race and racism, illustrating his thoughts with research from a range of academic and artistic disciplines, such as history, sociology, anthropology, biology, literature, films and the performing arts. The author's inclusion of ideas from other disciplines accords with my own thinking on the subject. In particular, race and racism are powerful group phenomena, and hence would appear to benefit from a multi-theoretical dialogue, in order to analyse more fully and understand their various processes and effects.

The book is written in a fresh, engaging manner, and is divided into three main sections: historical, theoretical and clinical. There are fifteen chapters with interesting titles which captivate the imagination and encourage one to read.
